title: Reality Fracture’s best cards in Magic: The Gathering

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Magic: The Gathering’s (MTG) multiversal saga headlined by Jace Beleren is coming to a head with its latest Standard expansion, Reality Fracture releasing on October 2, 2026.

What if the Multiverse existed without the suffering, Eldrazi, and Phyrexians that shaped its history? Reality Fracture explores those possibilities through the Echoverse, a warped reflection of the Multiverse created by Jace.

That idea extends to the set’s cards, with familiar characters and concepts receiving drastically different versions of themselves. From changes in abilities and effects to characters taking on entirely different colors, Reality Fracture puts a new spin on some of Magic’s most recognizable faces.
As the global release comes closer, here are some of the cards worth keeping an eye on as Reality Fracture makes its way into players’ hands.

Blue
The Theorist, Jace Beleren
Realistically, the big bad of this set and the protagonist of MTG for the longest time, The Theorist, Jace Beleren acts as the set’s poster boy, and with good reason.

With a built-in draw engine that gains you a card during each opponent’s draw phase, an ability that leaves a creature behind, a way to interact with a creature or artifact under each opponent’s control, and a pseudo-game-winning ultimate that draws cards and strengthens your creatures, The Theorist puts theories into practice, creating card advantage without skipping a beat.

While it’s obvious that multiplayer formats like Commander were taken into consideration with the “each opponent” wording found in his abilities, the real heat comes from the alternate versions of cards found throughout the set.
Perfected Theory
Perfected Theory lives up to its namesake and turns into an efficient piece of removal, while making combat more difficult for your opponent.
With the prevalence of prowess-based strategies in literally every format, Perfected Theory is the card you have to play around once you see blue.
Turning a normal turn into a blowout is a common sight in Modern Prowess, and doing it sooner makes the deck a faster matchup than it normally is.
Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun
Cited as being the card that would probably ruin competitive Commander, Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun is one of many echoed pairs found throughout the expansion.
While its red counterpart gives all creatures you control haste, the blue Samut doesn’t let your opponent react, granting all your instants and sorceries split second.

There’s no denying that it would shake up the meta in one way or another. Being blue, though, does make it more relevant in older formats, serving as a pitchable card for Force of Will and Force of Negation.
Green
Hexhaven Invigorator
A riff on Phyrexian Obliterator from way back in the early days of New Phyrexia, Hexhaven Invigorator is one of the most–if not the most–broken cards in the set.
Green continues to show why it’s the creature color with an efficient beater, with four green mana already creating a 6/6 threat with vigilance, but the effect makes it a bit over the top.

For each damage that Hexhaven Invigorator takes, it lets its owner get any land from their deck tapped. While it would be fine getting basic lands, having the flexibility to get tech lands or win-cons like Valakut, The Molten Pinnacle make this card a must remove threat.
Carnivorous Cultivator
Fetchlands are a quintessential part of MTG as formats get deeper, and in slower formats, a creature that can recur lands while accruing value is always worth watching.

Carnivorous Cultivator joins green’s roster of land searchers alongside Elvish Reclaimer and Crop Rotation. While it may be on the slower side, being able to recur lands with a creature that’s difficult to block thanks to deathtouch can generate plenty of value over the course of a game.
Pia, Aether Ascetic

Pia, Aether Ascetic is an enchantment tutor in colors that shouldn’t be able to find them that easily. While green does have a semblance of enchantment support, this is usually through Aura effects needing a creature in play.

Pia ignores the normal play pattern established by green, giving its user the flexibility to get key enchantments as it enters the battlefield like removal such as Oblivion Ring or a bomb like Omniscience.
Black
Darklight Phoenix
An alternate take on Arclight Phoenix, Darklight Phoenix spins the entire Arclight effect of coming back from the graveyard ready to attack.

Triggering off multiple instances of instants and sorceries and shifting over to deaths puts Darklight in a unique spot. Unlike its predecessor, it counts instances specifically creature deaths in general and not just those on your side. The original Arclight Phoenix strategy dominated the Standard metagame and is still a valid strategy in Pioneer, but Darklight Phoenix has a bright future ahead of itself once the right home materializes.
Sanctum Lurker
Cards that break rules are always bound to be broken, and Sanctum Lurker breaks the foundational rule of planeswalkers existing even without any loyalty counters.
While it has an awkward statline for its mana cost, it allows Superfriends decks to not only keep their planeswalker army safe during combat, but also enables some potentially broken synergies.
One example is Gideon Jura. With Sanctum Lurker in play, you can continuously use Gideon’s plus-two ability to force your opponent’s creatures to attack it.

Normally, a planeswalker with no loyalty counters would be sent to the graveyard. Sanctum Lurker prevents that from happening, allowing Gideon to remain on the battlefield and use the same ability again on the following turn.
Lich’s Relic
Equipment in MTG is only as good as the creature wielding it, but in the case of Lich’s Relic, its value when it enters.
For an additional two mana upon entry, Lich’s Relic lets its user destroy a creature or planeswalker per player currently in the game.
While it resembles the common Crude Bent Blade from The Hobbit, being able to bypass player hexproof and destroy planeswalkers justifies its higher rarity.
It gets even better when the artifact is cycled with cards like Goblin Welder or Goblin Engineer, letting the destruction effect happen more than once.
Red
Curse-Marred Demon
An alternate version of Rune-Scarred Demon, Curse-Marred Demon is a decent beater with a tutor stapled onto it.
At 4/4 for four mana, this red Demon with flying and trample enters the battlefield with a Gamble stapled onto it.
This lets you search for any card from your deck in exchange for discarding a card at random.

A searcher attached to a sizable body is always a great thing to have, and with how prevalent graveyard strategies are, as well as the existence of abilities like Madness and Mayhem, getting a guaranteed spell at a discount is always a good.
Identity Echo
Polymorph and other similar effects are strong in the context of MTG, oftentimes cheating something unfair into play way before it normally should. Identity Echo continues that trend.
Similar to the play patterns established by the red sorcery Indomitable Creativity, Identity Echo could transform any creature or planeswalker into another one found in the deck.
With the right deck design, normally weak tokens like Dwarves from Dwarven Mine or even Jace tokens could turn into game-ending threats like Emrakul or Nicol Bolas.
Pyre Rhymer
Taking a page out of Strixhaven with the Prepared mechanic, Pyre Rhymer offers a red ritual effect in the same vein as Molten Tide’s originator, High Tide.
Apart from coming with a 3/3 body for three mana that gets bigger with each noncreature spell cast thanks to prowess, it also comes prepared with Molten Tide ready to be cast on the following turn.

While there are no obvious homes for it at the time of writing, costing three mana in a color that could potentially have it ready by turn two with the various ritual effects available makes it something to be wary of.
White
Guiding Hydra
Hydras are often found in the green spectrum of MTG, with white being a supplementary color, like Progenitus. Guiding Hydra changes all that.

Reality Fracture breaks the normal Hydra mold, featuring a creature that not only acts as a mana sink from turn two onwards but also provides an anthem effect every turn, granting each other creature on its controller’s side of the battlefield +1/+1 counters.
This is something that white go-wide strategies would gladly accept.
Flickering Hound
As an alternate version of Displacer Kitten, Flickering Hound at four mana enables degenerate combos given the right circumstances.
In lieu of noncreature spells triggering a flicker effect for nonland permanents, including creatures, Flickering Hound does the same for creatures, flickering another creature upon casting a spell.

While the combo applications aren’t as wide, being able to generate value from other creatures entering the battlefield in dedicated creature decks is something to be wary of, making this a potential must-have for any creature-based Commander deck with white down the line.
Loyal Tutor
One-mana tutors have always been strong in their own right, with Worldly Tutor and Enlightened Tutor being two notable examples.
This set introduces Loyal Tutor specifically for planeswalkers.

In the right deck, a one-mana silver-bullet finder is invaluable, and with strategies that can crumble under the presence of key walkers like Teferi, Time Raveler and Narset, Parter of Veils, Loyal Tutor will definitely be seeing play in planeswalker-centric strategies.
Multicolor
Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes

Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes seems like a boring card, letting you empower Jace tokens as you play lands. As Jace ticks up thanks to empower you get to occasionally draw a card after playing two lands or mill one card a turn.

As you move into formats with fetchlands, this steady stream of advantage can get overwhelming. Even with just one additional card per turn, decks like the Azorius Loki strategy in Modernshow that every draw matters.
It also helps that there’s a planeswalker that would need to be dealt with even without the Avatar.
Solitary Cell
Red-white control decks have it good with all the removal options being printed recently, and Solitary Cell just strengthens already existing strategies.
On entry, it removes any nonland permanent with mana value three or less, while its cycling effect lets you turn excess legends into value.
Solitary Cell also makes Oswald Fiddlebender-based decks more fluid, giving them a removal option at two mana while continuing the artifact chain.
Aerid Konstrari
The Konstrari (R/G) is what happens when Jace alters the Prismari (U/R) school of thought, ditching instants and sorceries for artifacts.
This Gruul (R/G)-coded Elder Sphinx is an efficient cost beater that practically just costs three mana when you take its Heartwood token into consideration.

Apart from being an infinite enters-the-battlefield trigger with Food Chain in Commander, it also lends itself to being a fun build-around card considering there will always be artifact synergies laying around.
Special Mentions
Emrakul, the Exigent Doom
Emrakul is the only colorless card in the set and a fitting endgame in Reality Fracture’s story.
Emrakul, the Exigent Doom does two things and does them really well. It accelerates your mana generation by turning any of your lands into two colorless mana for use in the future.
This effect can give you a late-game threat your opponents have to be wary of.
Somewhat of a game-ender while still supporting big-mana strategies, Emrakul is going to be a card you’ll want in your collection regardless of your format.
Tarmogoyf
Once regarded as one of the strongest cards in MTG, Tarmogoyf finally enters the Standard card pool after an absence of almost two decades.
While it may not be the titan it once was, being in a lower-power environment in Standard, and to a minor extent Pioneer, may let it resemble the terror it once was.
Times have changed, with removal improving heavily, but that won’t stop players from forcing Tarmogoyf when there are better things to do with two mana.
Is Reality Fracture a good set competitively, casually, and for collectors?
While Jace Beleren’s time in MTG is legendary, from the onset, Reality Fracture is shaping up to be an all-timer set, complete with a mechanic that could see use years from now in Empower.
The card quality present has considerations for every format, with some cards like Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun sure to shake things up once they become legal.
Even the presence of Tarmogoyf in the format gives longtime players a reason to celebrate, as they can dust off their old copies that have been lying in wait.
MTG’s second-to-last set of the year has all the tools to make an impact across every format.
Whether it’s through Empower, power creep, or the sheer number of new tools available to players, Reality Fracture has plenty to offer players of every caliber.
For collectors, the set’s special printings, alternate versions, and bundles add another layer of appeal beyond the cards themselves.
Reality Fracture is set to have its global release on October 2, 2026, with prereleases happening from September 25, 2026 onwards.
